CARD GRADING SUBMISSION PICKER · RUNS IN YOUR BROWSER

Is it worth grading? Which of these cards should you send, and which should you sell raw?

Grading fees, shipping and weeks of waiting eat the premium on most cards. Paste your cards with what each would sell for raw and at each grade, and your own chance of each grade, and get the expected net from grading against selling raw, the cheapest fee tier that covers each card, the exact chance of a 10 each card needs to be worth sending, the downside, and — if you have a budget or a card limit per submission — the exact best subset to send.

Your estimates, not a price guide and not a forecast. This page knows no card prices and predicts no grades: every value, chance, fee and turnaround is a number you type. For Pokemon, baseball, basketball, football and Magic sellers and collectors using PSA, BGS, CGC, SGC or any grader. Nothing is uploaded: the text boxes are analysed in this browser and never leave your device.

1. Paste your cards

2. Your grader's fee tiers

3. The submission

Send to the grader (best first)

#CardTierFee + shippingExpected net gradedNet selling rawExpected gainNeeds a 10 chance ofYou saidChance worse than rawWorst case vs raw

Sell raw or hold

CardWhyExpected gain from gradingNeeds a 10 chance ofYou said

Against simple rules

RuleCardsGrading spendExpected gain over raw

    Nothing here is a prediction. Expected net is your own numbers multiplied out; any single card can come back at a grade you did not expect.

    Prefer a CLI?

    Same logic, zero dependencies, one command — reads a file or stdin:

    node cli.mjs pick cards.csv --budget 400 --max-cards 20 --ship 8
cat cards.csv | node cli.mjs pick - --tiers my-tiers.csv --json

    Get cli.mjs and engine.mjs — Node 18+, nothing to install, no network call. More: Is it worth grading a card? The break-even math.

    What's recognised

    InputHandling

    The answer is exact for the numbers you type (exact subset search under a budget or card limit, closed-form break-even). It does not know card prices, population reports, grader policies, pricing changes while your cards are away, loss or damage in transit, or what a slab will really sell for. A grading company's own rules about declared value, card types it accepts and turnaround come first.

    Common questions

    Is this a price guide or a grade predictor?

    No. Every card value, grade chance, grading fee and turnaround in the answer is a number you typed or an illustrative example you were told to replace. It does not look up prices, read a population report or judge a card from a photo. It does the arithmetic on your own estimates and shows you which cards need a better estimate.

    Does it upload my card list?

    No. The browser page works on the text you paste, in your own browser, and never sends it anywhere. The CLI reads a local file or stdin and makes no network call.

    How does it choose which cards to send?

    For each card it takes the cheapest fee tier whose declared-value limit covers the card's best case, then weighs what the card would sell for at each grade by your chance of that grade, subtracts the grading fee and shipping, discounts the wait, and compares that with selling the card raw today. Cards that beat raw are the candidates; if you set a budget or a cards-per-submission limit it finds the exact best subset rather than ranking and cutting off.

    What is the break-even chance of a 10?

    The chance of a gem-grade result at which grading and selling raw have the same expected net, holding your other grade chances fixed. It is solved exactly from the arithmetic, not searched for. Compare it with your own honest estimate: a card that needs 40 percent and that you rate at 10 percent is a pass.

    Are the fee tiers current?

    No. The built-in fee table is an example so the page works on first load. Graders change fees, declared-value limits and turnaround often. Copy the numbers from the grader's current price list into the table before you rely on the answer.

    Which cards and graders does it cover?

    Any card where you can estimate a raw value and a value at each grade: Pokemon, baseball, basketball, football, Magic: The Gathering and others, for PSA, BGS, CGC, SGC or any grader whose fees you enter.

    No warranty. This tool is provided free and as-is, without warranty of any kind, express or implied. It is not financial, tax, legal, investment or authentication advice, it is not a price guide or a grade prediction, and it does not replace a qualified professional or a grading company's own guidance. You are responsible for reviewing and verifying its output before relying on it, for the accuracy of the values, grade chances, fees and turnaround times you type, for any grader's current terms, and for any loss or damage to cards sent in the mail. Card values move, and grading can return a lower grade than you expect. To the maximum extent permitted by law, the authors accept no liability for any loss or damage arising from its use. It chooses between options using the numbers you supply; it is not a forecast of what will happen to a card.

    Not affiliated with, endorsed by or sponsored by PSA, BGS, Beckett, CGC, SGC or any grading company or marketplace; their names are used only to say which services the tool can be fed numbers for.

    Best-effort hosting, no SLA. These tools are free, experimental, and may be slow, broken, moved, or taken offline without notice. We do not promise uptime, backups of anything you type, or that a URL will keep working. Do not use this as a system of record. If a tool needs to survive, get cli.mjs and run it yourself.

    Everything runs in your browser. The text you paste is never uploaded; there are no accounts, cookies, or analytics vendors. Anonymous feature events (pick_run, example_loaded) are counted only in local storage and can be deleted with the button below. Do Not Track and Global Privacy Control are honoured.

    Related tools on the same repo: eBay Fee Calculator, Marketplace Fee Compare, Lot Split Calculator and Ticket Resale Profit Calculator.

is-it-worth-grading-a-card.html.text:
Card Grading Submission Picker · guide

Is it worth grading a card? The break-even chance of a 10

Short answer: grade a card when your own chance of a high grade is above the break-even chance for that card, which you can work out exactly from what the card sells for raw and at each grade, the grading fee, shipping, the marketplace fee and the wait. The picker does that for a whole list, and finds the best set when you have a budget or a limit on cards per submission.

Everything below is arithmetic on invented numbers. The values, grade chances and fee tiers are illustrative, not prices, not a price guide and not a forecast. Replace them with your own.

The arithmetic

  1. Selling raw nets the raw price less the marketplace fee, today.
  2. Grading nets, for each grade, the slab's sale price less the marketplace fee, discounted for the weeks it took, less the grading fee and shipping and insurance. Weight each grade by your chance of it. Whatever your chances of 10, 9 and 8 do not use up is grade 7 or lower.
  3. The uplift is the second number minus the first. Grade the card if it is positive.
  4. The break-even chance of a 10 is the chance at which the uplift is exactly zero with your other chances held fixed. It is linear in the chance of a 10, so it has a closed form.

A worked list

Thirteen cards across Pokemon, baseball, basketball, football and Magic, with example fee tiers (a $25 economy tier up to $500 declared, up to a $600 elite tier up to $20,000), $8 shipping and insurance a card, a 13 percent marketplace fee plus $0.30, and a 10 percent annual discount rate for the wait. Every figure is invented.

  • With no budget the picker sends 8 of 13 cards for $1,189.00 in fees and shipping, expected $2,405.21 above selling them raw. Four cards lose to raw (a common holo and a whitened rookie by the most, a vintage card narrowly), and one card is worth $24,000 at best, above every tier in the table, so it is flagged rather than guessed at.
  • A $260 raw card whose 10 is worth $900 and 9 is worth $420, rated at a 5 percent chance of a 10, needs about 5.4 percent. Expected gain from grading is -$2.03, so it stays raw. At a 7 percent chance it would go.
  • With a $400 budget the exact best subset is 3 cards for $374.00, expected $1,512.77 above raw. Sending the highest-value cards first within the same budget gives $1,360.88, so the best subset is $151.89 better.
  • The elite-tier card has the biggest single gain, but the $608.00 in fees and shipping does not fit a $400 budget at all, and the picker says so.

Reading the downside

An expected gain hides the bad outcomes. For every card the picker also prints the chance, on your own odds, of ending below selling raw, and the worst case against raw. The Charizard-style card in the example has a 15 percent chance of ending worse than raw and, at a grade 7 or lower, would come out $302.87 behind selling raw.

What to feed it

  1. Raw value and the value at each grade from sold listings you trust, not asking prices.
  2. Your honest chance of each grade, from looking at corners, edges, surface and centering. Be conservative: the picker multiplies exactly what you give it.
  3. The fee tiers, declared-value limits and turnaround from the grader's current price list, plus your shipping and insurance per card.

A grader's own rules about accepted cards, declared value and turnaround come first.

Questions

Is it worth grading a card?

Only if the expected sale price of the slab, after the grading fee, shipping, marketplace fees and the wait, beats what the raw card would net today. That depends on your own chances of each grade, so the useful question is how likely a high grade has to be before grading wins. The picker solves that exactly for each card.

What chance of a PSA 10 do I need for grading to pay?

It depends on the gap between the 10 price and the 9 and below, and on the fee tier. On the worked list, a $260 raw card whose 10 is worth $900 and 9 is worth $420 needs about a 5.4 percent chance of a 10 once fees, shipping and the wait are included. A card whose 10 is only a little more than raw needs a chance you cannot honestly claim.

Which grading tier should I pick?

The cheapest tier whose declared-value limit covers the card's best case. Declared value limits and fees change, so the picker ships a labelled example table that you replace with the grader's current price list.

Why does a budget make the answer different?

Because ranking by gain and cutting off is not the same as the best use of a fixed budget. A single expensive tier can displace two cards that together gain more. With a budget or a card limit the picker searches subsets exactly.

No warranty. This guide is provided free and as-is, without warranty of any kind. It is not financial, tax, legal, investment or authentication advice, and it is not a price guide or a grade prediction. You are responsible for verifying its output, for the numbers you enter, and for any loss or damage to cards sent in the mail. The worked example is illustrative arithmetic on invented numbers, not a forecast.

Best-effort hosting, no SLA. These tools are free, experimental, and may be slow, broken, moved, or taken offline without notice. Do not use this as a system of record.

Free and open source (MIT). Support is optional and never changes what the tool does.
